title: Alpine Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Alpine wells have a 61 ft median depth, 13 gpm median yield, and estimated finished-well costs of $9,000-$16,600.
h1: What Alpine Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
For rural property in Alpine and nearby Gerrard or South Fork, the local well records show a wide range of conditions. The median reported depth is 61 feet, but the middle half runs from 45 to 210 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,600 feet.

Reported production is generally useful: the median pump yield is 13.0 gallons per minute. That is encouraging, but the records are not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. Before buying, compare nearby permits, confirm the intended use with Colorado DWR, and budget for the actual ground, access, pump system, trenching, and electrical work.

sections.heading: Alpine well depths vary sharply by ground and aquifer
sections.html:
Depth records around Alpine are weighted toward relatively shallow wells. About 61% are under 100 feet, while 21% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 15% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 4% exceed 600 feet.

For a drilling bid, the 61-foot median is a useful starting point, not a promise. The middle-half range of 45 to 210 feet shows why a neighboring well at a similar address may still not predict your exact depth. Permits commonly identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock conditions, along with the Unconfined San Luis Valley aquifer. Fractured ground can change quickly over short distances, so a driller should review nearby logs and access conditions before setting a price.

sections.heading: Alpine well yields are usually adequate, but not uniform
sections.html:
Among the Alpine-area records that report pump yield, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The distribution is split between stronger and moderate wells: 46% report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 45% fall from 5 to 15 gallons per minute.

Low-yield wells are not the dominant pattern, but they are part of the local risk. About 7% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 2% report under 1 gallon per minute. A buyer should ask how yield was measured and whether the result supports the planned home, livestock, irrigation, or other use. A storage tank can help manage a slower well, but it does not create more groundwater.

sections.heading: Water levels around Alpine do not show a simple steady decline
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 30 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 14 to 87 feet. That range matters for pump setting, construction planning, and understanding how much lift the system may need. Static level is measured when the well is not being pumped and is different from the depth of the well itself.

The decade pattern is mixed rather than a straight downward trend. The median was 30 feet in the 2000s, 42 feet in the 2010s, and 30 feet in the 2020s. Only 165 records report a static water level, so this is useful local context but not a complete groundwater study. Have the driller check the specific parcel and nearby well logs before relying on a regional median.

sections.heading: Alpine has a long permit history and recurring local drillers
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 2,037 permitted wells within the mapped area, with 1,431 recorded as constructed. Permitting activity was highest in the 1990s, with 482 permits, followed by 468 in the 2000s. The newest permit year in the records is 2026, so the area continues to see well activity.

The most frequent names in the records are Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.), with 413 wells; American Drilling Service (Dewberry, Bradford W.), with 256; and L D Spencer Drilling And Pump (Spencer, Lonnie D.), with 118. These records show who has worked locally, but you should still confirm current licensing, availability, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: A median-depth Alpine well can cost $9,000 to $16,600 finished
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. Drilling is estimated at $50 to $75 per foot. At the 61-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at roughly $3,000 to $4,600.

A usable water system costs more than the hole. The estimated finished-well range, including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, is $9,000 to $16,600 at the median depth. A shallow estimate should not be treated as a fixed bid: difficult access, casing and grout requirements, deeper drilling, fractured rock, water testing, and site-specific electrical or trench work can change the total. Get the written scope before comparing bids, especially on undeveloped land near South Fork or Gerrard.

sections.heading: Check Alpine contamination, dry-hole, septic, and building risks
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 64 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapping. Those figures do not prove that a particular well is safe or unsafe. Test the water from an existing well, and ask a qualified professional what testing fits the parcel and its nearby land uses.

Low yield and a dry hole remain possible even where nearby wells produce well. Septic setbacks, driveway layout, building location, and well access need to work together before construction starts. Confirm the permit and intended household use with Colorado DWR. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required, and an exempt household-use well still has a 35-gpm pumping limit. Review the actual permit rather than assuming a neighbor's rights transfer to your property.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Alpine, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Alpine is 61 feet. The middle half of wells ranges from 45 to 210 feet. About 61% are under 100 feet, but the deepest record reaches 1,600 feet. Those figures show a broad local range, so a driller should review nearby well logs and the parcel's ground conditions before quoting a final depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Alpine, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 61-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,000 to $4,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,000 to $16,600. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing, grout, and site-specific work can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Alpine wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield near Alpine is 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 46% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Low-yield records still occur: 7% are from 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 2% are under 1 gallon per minute.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Alpine, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water from a particular Alpine property is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 64 historic mine features. Test an existing well before purchase and test a new well after construction. Review the results with a qualified water professional.

faq.q: Do I need a permit or augmentation plan for an Alpine well?
faq.a: Colorado DWR records show 2,037 permitted wells in the mapped Alpine area, and the newest permit year is 2026. A household-use well may qualify as an exempt well, but the actual permit controls its use. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. Confirm the parcel's water status and planned use with Colorado DWR before building.
